  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Vignette:
Six months ago, Arjun Kapoor was walking through the district near the old market when a man stepped out from behind a delivery truck. He didn’t call out. He just closed the distance quickly and pressed something hard against Arjun’s ribs. The stranger’s breath was thick with fermented spirits. Arjun handed over his wallet and phone, hands steady but heart hammering, as the man turned and vanished into the evening traffic. Arjun had spent his life working with circuits and currents, but that night he learned how quickly a body could feel like a live wire. In the weeks that followed, the past did not stay behind. Arjun began waking up from a nightmare with the phantom pressure of an arm across his chest and the taste of copper in his mouth. He would sit on the edge of his bed until his breathing evened out, certain the nightmare was simply trying to catch up to him. When he stepped out, the narrow walkways of the neighborhood grocery store felt suddenly inescapable. He began taking the long way around, keeping his shoulders rolled forward, because too many bodies moving at once made his pulse jump. On Tuesdays, when he met his crew for coffee, he found himself leaning away from the table whenever a new customer walked in. A faint whiff of bourbon or cheap rum near his work truck made his jaw tighten. He knew better than to dismiss it. It was the same smell. He didn’t need a weapon to remember what the encounter had felt like. Nights became the hardest stretch of the day. While his wife, Priya, slept beside him, Arjun stayed awake, listening to the settling house and the distant highway. He had come to believe that darkness was a blank canvas where the mind filled in the gaps, so he kept a small lamp on in the hallway and locked the deadbolt twice. During the day, his caution didn’t fade. When a neighbor’s teenager jogged up the driveway to ask for directions, Arjun’s shoulders shot up before his brain could catch up. He was certain that strangers moving quickly toward him were never asking for help. A casual wave from a delivery driver, a sudden turn of a corner on a job site, anything that broke his line of sight put him on immediate guard. He didn’t jump; he just went still, calculating angles, waiting to see if the movement was friendly or final. The adjustments accumulated quietly. Arjun stopped volunteering for the after-dark retrofit jobs that used to pay well. He began asking his foreman to assign him only to morning calls in familiar commercial buildings. When Priya invited friends over for dinner, he left early, saying he had an early call, because the clinking of glasses and the murmur of conversations made his skin feel too tight. The work shifted too. He passed up a contract to rewire a downtown high-rise because the service elevator opened directly into a packed lobby, and he couldn’t risk the crush around the stairwell. His wife noticed the quiet distance he kept, the way he measured every doorway and every approaching footstep. She tried to talk to him about it, but he didn’t have the words for the weight he carried. At seventy-six, Arjun had always prided himself on being the one who fixed things. Lately, however, he found himself waiting for the right moment to step outside, rehearsing exits before entering rooms, and waking hours before dawn just to sit in the kitchen until the light changed. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the certainty that his body would never stop bracing. He had come to believe that if he finally let his guard down, he would be caught off guard again. So he made the call to the community clinic, hoping someone could help him untangle the wires in his own head. He didn’t want to be a prisoner of his own nerves, and he wanted to know if he could ever sit through a full evening without checking the door three times.
